Bernedoodle Planning: Size Ranges, Coat, and Parent Breeds

Planning a Bernedoodle means studying its parent breeds. A practical look at size variability, coat care, health questions, and a cost plan from local quotes.

Published: 2026-10-29Sources checked: 3Educational planning guide

A Bernedoodle is a Bernese Mountain Dog and Poodle cross, so the most useful planning starts with the parent breeds: expect wide variation in size, real grooming demands, and health questions you take to the parents' testing records rather than to marketing.

Why the parent breeds decide almost everything

A Bernedoodle is not a standardized breed, so its size, coat, and temperament are inherited from its two parent breeds and can vary widely even within a single litter. That makes the parent breeds your best evidence. The Bernese Mountain Dog, per VCA Animal Hospitals, is a large Swiss breed roughly 23 to 28 inches tall, 70 to 120 pounds, with a life expectancy of about 6 to 9 years, an easygoing, devoted companion that learns quickly, tends to be aloof toward strangers, and is good with children and other pets when supervised.

VCA also notes the Bernese enjoys cold weather but does not do well in warm weather, and that the breed tends to stay in good weight or slightly overweight, so calorie control matters. Poodles, the other parent, come in standard, miniature, and toy sizes, which is why Bernedoodles are marketed across a huge size range and why a curly, lower-shedding coat is often part of the appeal.

Because there is no single standard, ask the breeder about both parents specifically rather than trusting a size label like "mini" or "standard." Two Bernedoodles from different breeders can be as different as a large dog and a small one, with very different food, space, and cost needs.

Planning for size you cannot fully predict

Since a Bernedoodle's adult size depends on which Poodle size was used and on the individual puppy, plan for a range rather than a number. A cross involving a Standard Poodle and a Bernese Mountain Dog can produce a large dog approaching the Bernese end of the scale; a Miniature Poodle cross tends smaller. Ask the breeder for the measured adult weights of both parents and previous litters, and prepare your home, car, and budget for the upper end of the likely range so you are not caught off guard.

Size affects far more than looks. It drives how much the dog eats, the crate and equipment you buy, boarding and daycare rates, medication doses, and even whether the dog can travel in-cabin or must go in cargo. VCA's note that the Bernese does poorly in warm weather is also worth remembering: a large, dense-coated Bernedoodle may share that heat sensitivity, so plan cool-hour exercise in summer and ask your veterinarian about warm-weather care.

Our size chart and budget guide shows how weight drives food, equipment, and boarding costs, and giant-breed car transport is worth reading if a large parent is involved.

Coat care is the recurring commitment

Bernedoodles are often chosen for a wavy or curly, lower-shedding coat inherited from the Poodle side, but that same coat typically needs regular brushing and professional grooming to prevent matting. For reference on the Bernese side, VCA says the Bernese coat is moderately long, either slightly wavy or straight, and needs brushing once or twice weekly, more when shedding, with above-average shedding. A Bernedoodle's actual coat can fall anywhere between the two parents, so the puppy you meet may not predict the adult coat you get.

A curlier, Poodle-type coat usually means the most grooming work of all: frequent at-home brushing plus a groomer visit every few weeks to keep the coat from matting into painful clumps. Neglected curly coats often end up shaved down, which defeats the reason many owners chose the coat in the first place. Treat professional grooming as a recurring, non-optional cost, not an occasional luxury.

No dog is guaranteed hypoallergenic. Our hypoallergenic reality check and doodle grooming cost questions explain why a curlier coat usually means more, not less, grooming work and expense. Interview a groomer before committing; the grooming salon interview helps you ask the right things.

Cost worksheet that accounts for grooming

The line most owners underestimate is professional grooming, which recurs every few weeks for a coated dog. Price everything locally and against the likely upper size.

LineFormula to fill with local quotes
Setupcrate sized to expected adult + bed + slicker brush and comb + initial veterinary exam quote
Monthly food(measured daily portion for the expected adult weight x cost per unit) x 30
Monthly groominggroomer price per visit / weeks between visits x 4.3, plus at-home brushing supplies
Annual care(monthly food + monthly grooming + parasite prevention) x 12 + wellness exam + vaccine quote
Reservefund for orthopedic or other care; ask your clinic for a written estimate

Move the annual figure into the five-year cost framework and size the buffer with the emergency fund formula. The grooming line is the one most likely to surprise you: for a coated dog it recurs every few weeks for the dog's whole life, so multiply it out over years, not months, before you decide.

Watch two size-driven traps in the worksheet. First, a large Bernedoodle eats and doses like a large dog, so do not budget using a small-dog friend's numbers. Second, if a large parent is involved, the crate, car setup, boarding rate, and even some medications scale up. Pricing the upper end of the size range keeps you from being caught short if the puppy grows bigger than expected.

A realistic grooming month

Test the commitment over a month, not a day. Each week you brush and comb thoroughly to prevent mats, especially behind the ears, under the legs, and around the collar where friction creates tangles fastest. Every four to eight weeks you visit a groomer for a trim, or you learn to do it yourself with equipment and time. Between visits you check ears and keep the coat free of tangles that can become painful mats close to the skin.

Now imagine skipping a few weeks during a busy stretch. A curly coat can mat quickly, and once mats form tight against the skin, brushing them out is painful and a groomer may have no choice but to shave the dog short. That is the moment many owners realize the low-shedding coat they chose is also a high-commitment one. Building a steady weekly habit, and a standing groomer appointment, is what keeps the coat comfortable.

If that rhythm sounds like more than you want, a lower-maintenance coat may suit you better. The grooming, not the puppy price, is often the biggest ongoing surprise for new coated-dog owners, and it is worth being honest about before you bring a dog home.

Health questions to take to the parents' records

Because a Bernedoodle inherits risks from both sides, screening of the parents matters. The Cornell Riney Canine Health Center advises verifying health testing on the OFA website and buying from breeders who complete recommended screening and offer lifelong support. Cornell's hip dysplasia page notes the condition is common in medium and large breeds and stresses screening and healthy weight. Ask the breeder:

  • Were both parents hip- and elbow-screened, and can I confirm results on OFA?
  • What eye and other testing did each parent complete?
  • What are the measured adult sizes of both parents?
  • Will you take the dog back if my circumstances change?

Ask your veterinarian how to feed a growing pup to protect joints, especially if a large parent is involved.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a fixed size. Adult size depends on the Poodle size used and the individual dog.
  • Expecting no shedding or allergy-free. No dog is guaranteed hypoallergenic, and coats vary.
  • Underbudgeting grooming. A curly coat usually means recurring professional grooming.
  • Skipping parent health records. Verify both parents' screening on OFA.

What this guide cannot tell you

Because a Bernedoodle is a cross rather than a standardized breed, no guide can predict your individual dog's adult size, coat type, temperament, or health; those depend on the specific parents and on chance. The parent-breed facts here come from veterinary sources and describe those breeds in general. This is not medical advice. Rely on the parents' documented health testing, an honest breeder, and your own veterinarian, and gather local quotes for the cost worksheet.

FAQ

How big will a Bernedoodle get?
It depends on which Poodle size was used and on the individual puppy, so there is no single answer. The Bernese Mountain Dog parent is large, roughly 70 to 120 pounds per VCA, while Poodles range from toy to standard. Ask the breeder for the measured adult weights of both parents and past litters, and plan your home, car, and budget for the upper end of the likely range.
Are Bernedoodles hypoallergenic and low-shedding?
No dog can be guaranteed hypoallergenic. Many Bernedoodles inherit a wavy or curly, lower-shedding coat from the Poodle side, but coats vary within a litter and can resemble either parent. A curlier coat usually needs more grooming, not less. If allergies are a concern, spend time with the specific dog first and speak with your physician about your own sensitivities.
What health testing should the parents have?
Cornell advises verifying screening on the OFA website and choosing breeders who complete recommended testing. For a Bernese-and-Poodle cross, ask whether both parents were hip- and elbow-screened and had eye testing, and confirm the results online. Also ask about conditions seen in each line. This does not diagnose your future dog, but it lowers the odds of inherited problems and signals a responsible breeder.
